## Chapter 39: Brainstorming and Process Improvement Tools

### Activity Network Diagram

An activity network diagram helps a Six Sigma team map both the activities involved in a project and the activities involved in a process. The diagram's goal is to understand the sequential and time-based relationships within a project or process. Which items come first? Which activities happen at the same time?

When applied to an overall project, the activity network diagram helps teams and project leaders understand which resources will be needed at each point during the project. It can also give project managers a better ability to estimate timelines.

When applied to a process, the diagram helps teams identify every activity in a process. It also helps teams understand which activities are upstream and downstream, and which activities happen together. Once teams know these things, they can start discussing whether the current sequence is the most effective and understand how changes to one activity might impact another activity's outcome.

An activity network diagram is created by following these steps:

1. List every activity involved in the process. Teams can draw on their own knowledge or on tools used previously by the group, like a SIPOC or process maps.
2. Write each activity on a separate card or sticky note.
3. Place the activities in order from left to right. Activities that are simultaneous are placed in a vertical line within a single horizontal space on the diagram.
4. Write an estimated time for each activity.
5. Trace a critical path line through each step. Where there are vertical (simultaneous) steps, the line passes through whichever step takes longer.
6. Add up the times listed along the critical path to get a sense of the process's overall time estimate. In the example below, the critical path's total time, in minutes, is: 5 + 2 + 12 + 9 + 10 + 5, or 43.

### Affinity Diagram

An affinity diagram is a tool that lets the team list and group a large number of ideas quickly and systematically. Affinity diagrams work well when you're approaching a process or idea for the first time, because they help organize all the associated ideas to identify some of the main points the team will need to consider throughout the DMAIC project. Affinity diagrams are also a good tool to use if you have a larger-than-normal brainstorming group, which means they can be used in department meetings or in DMAIC meetings that include subject-matter experts who aren't part of the core team. The goal of an affinity diagram is to help the group understand the relationships between inputs, outputs, products, services, workers, customers, processes, and ideas — or any subgroup of these things.

To run an affinity diagram, you'll need a large workspace, like a table, wall, or floor. You can also use a whiteboard, and, if you're working with a group across multiple locations, you can run the exercise through web-conferencing software, though, as with most brainstorming tools, that isn't ideal.

An affinity diagram session is run by following the steps described below.

1. Give everyone in the session small cards, sticky notes, or pieces of paper.
2. Start brainstorming ideas about the process or problem. Ideas at this stage are pretty loose — encourage the team to write down anything that comes to mind. Ideas should be short — a word or two, or very simple phrases, otherwise the team might be logging two ideas on the same card. Encourage participants to log inputs, outputs, challenges, obstacles, customers, people, processes, actions, etc. If you're trying to address a specific question, that question should guide the kind of things logged on the notes.
3. Brainstorming can happen individually for a few minutes, or as a group. Individual brainstorming tends to produce a series of ideas uninfluenced by other people's input, which can be valuable.
4. After brainstorming, have everyone spread the cards out on the floor or table, or stick the notes on a wall or whiteboard.
5. Work as a team to identify related ideas. Place those ideas close to each other. Consider working as a team without talking during this step, moving ideas around the diagram for a few minutes, until most of the ideas are grouped into larger clusters.
6. If an idea could belong to more than one group, make multiple cards with that idea, so it can be placed in multiple groups.
7. It's fine to have groups of just one item, when an idea doesn't seem to fit anywhere else.
8. Once every note is grouped, hold a discussion with the team to answer some questions:
   a. Are there patterns in the ideas?
   b. Does the diagram generate new ideas or clarify ideas or relationships?
   c. Do the ideas fit into natural sequences for processes or timelines?
   d. Do the ideas fit into natural cause groupings?
9. The questions asked and answered will depend on which process or overall issue the team is addressing with the affinity diagram.
10. Give each group of ideas a title, drawing out what seems to be the main idea of that grouping.
11. Record the diagram for later use. You can have someone copy it onto a piece of paper, convert it into a digital diagram, or simply take a photo to store with the team's other documents.

### Interrelationship Diagram

An interrelationship diagram is similar, in purpose, to a fishbone diagram. The goal of interrelationship brainstorming is to understand which causes and effects are primary with respect to a problem or process. The outcome of the brainstorming session is a visual representation that makes it easy to see which items are likely causing most of the effects, and which effects are tied to which causes within a process.

As a Six Sigma specialist, you can deploy this exercise when teams don't fully understand the relationships between causes and effects within a process, can't agree on which causal factors might be primary within the process, or are just starting to understand the process and need more general knowledge before moving on to a fishbone diagram or measurement processes.

Run an interrelationship diagram session by following these steps:

1. Define the problem on a whiteboard, piece of paper, or sticky note.
2. On other sticky notes, write down ideas generated by brainstorming about the problem. Specifically: what could have caused the problem? What could be causing the things that cause the problems? What other problems could the problem cause?
3. Place the notes around the problem on the whiteboard.
4. As a team, consider each idea on each note. Decide whether that idea is related in any way to any other idea on the board.
5. If the idea is related to a second idea in a way that could cause it, or be an input or factor for it, draw an arrow going from the first idea to the one it could be an input, factor, or cause for.
6. If the idea is related to a second idea in a way that could be an effect or outcome of the second idea, draw an arrow going from the second idea to the first.
7. If needed, draw multiple arrows going in and out of each idea.
8. At the end of the exercise, count the number of arrows coming into each idea. Write those numbers in one color on each sticky note.
9. Count the number of arrows going out of each idea. Write those numbers in another color on each sticky note.
10. The notes with the highest total count — adding up those two numbers — are likely the key factors in the process or problem. You may also be able to identify key inputs (causes) and key outputs (effects) based on the number of arrows going in or out of various notes.

### Force Field Analysis

Much of Six Sigma education has to do with statistical analysis, but the methodology doesn't work if Six Sigma leaders get so caught up in numbers and data that they fail to notice people play an important role in every process, every project, and every improvement initiative. One way for Six Sigma teams to understand how people and other factors might support or challenge a process, project, or change is to run a force field analysis.

A force field analysis lets teams understand how the factors surrounding a process might support (or drive) change, or challenge (or restrain) change. Beyond people, factors can include culture, material and resource requirements, customers, needs, machines, rules, and regulations. Sometimes Six Sigma teams can work to change some of these factors, in order to build additional support for an improvement. In other cases, the team can't change the restraining factors, but should stay aware of those factors when moving forward with improvement initiatives.

Build a force field analysis by following these steps:

1. Start with the problem definition. This can be either the overall problem statement or a smaller, more detailed problem within the scope of the whole project.
2. Write the problem at the top of a whiteboard or large piece of paper.
3. Draw a thick line down the center of the page. This line represents the status quo — the process's current state.
4. Define the solution or desired state. If the team is just starting out, the desired state might be the project's overall goal statement. If the team is working to solve a specific problem within the project's scope, it may already have a solution in mind.
5. Write the solution or goal statement at the bottom of the whiteboard or page.
6. Brainstorm driving factors — factors that would move the status quo "forward."
7. Write the driving factors on the left side of the status quo line.
8. Brainstorm restraining factors — factors that would keep the status quo as it is.
9. Write the restraining factors on the right side of the status quo line.
10. Draw an arrow under each driving factor, pointing toward the status quo line; each arrow's length represents the driving factor's perceived strength. For example, the sponsor who holds the financial decisions is on board with the solution. That would be a strong driving factor and could get a long arrow.
11. Draw an arrow under each restraining factor, pointing back toward the status quo line. Each arrow's length represents the perceived strength of the challenge. If the sponsor weren't yet on board with the solution, that would be a fairly strong restraining factor.

Once the diagram is finished, the team can quickly see:

- Whether there are more driving or restraining factors
- Whether the driving or restraining factors carry more "weight" (based on the number of longer arrows on each side)
- Which factors are strongest

The team can then discuss whether any of the restraining factors can be weakened or converted into a driving factor, which can help clear the way for a smoother solution implementation.

### Responsibility Chart

A responsibility chart helps Six Sigma teams identify which people, teams, or departments have various types of connection or responsibility with respect to a process. The reason for understanding these relationships is to let Six Sigma teams understand who actually acts on or within the process, who needs to be kept informed about the process, who's ultimately accountable for the process, and who can offer valuable information about the process. Often, these various people can be identified with a mapping process known as RACI, which stands for:

- **Responsible** — the person or team that actually does the work (an employee responsible for taking money at the register)
- **Accountable** — the person in charge of the work (that shift's supervisor)
- **Consult** — anyone involved in steps before the activity who should be kept informed (the salesperson on the floor, the accountant who preps the registers at the start of each day)
- **Inform** — anyone involved in steps after the activity who should be kept informed (the accountant, who also counts the registers at the end of shifts)

Create a RACI chart for your project or process by following these steps:

1. Create a list of every activity and decision that's part of the process. Teams can draw this information from earlier brainstorming sessions or from tools like process maps.
2. List these items down the right side of a page or whiteboard.
3. Create a list of every functional role associated with a process. List them as row headers across the top of the page or whiteboard.
   a. Activities and decisions could include items like:
      i. Measure the wood.
      ii. Cut the wood.
      iii. Review the wood.
      iv. Decide whether the wood is the correct length.
   b. Functional roles could include:
      i. Wood measurer
      ii. Wood cutter
      iii. Auditor
      iv. Wood packer
4. For each functional role and activity, decide whether the role is Responsible or Accountable for each listed activity, or whether the role should be Consulted or Informed. In the example below, you can see the cutter is responsible for measuring and cutting, the auditor is responsible for reviewing and deciding whether the wood is correct, and the supervisor is accountable for all of it. The packer needs to be informed about whether the wood is correct, to know whether to package it.

### Nominal Group Technique

A Six Sigma leader needs to develop a solid understanding of group dynamics. Not every project team will function the same way, and Six Sigma leaders sometimes face interpersonal challenges within the group setting. Some of these challenges can derail brainstorming efforts because of personality conflicts. If you have one or more quiet or shy individuals, for example, you might not be getting their full perspective. Even if everyone on the team is reasonably participative, if there's a natural leader, a "bully," or a more talkative member, those people might be contributing more ideas than the others. One way to reduce the impact of personality on brainstorming sessions is to use the nominal group technique, to encourage input from everyone.

1. Give everyone a pen and paper.
2. Start with a question, topic, or concern relevant to the project or the phase you're in.
3. Set aside 5 to 10 minutes and invite everyone to brainstorm their own ideas. Make sure to make clear that, at this stage, there are no bad or wrong ideas.
4. As soon as everyone finishes writing, go around the table, asking each person to present one idea from their list. Each person should present only one idea at a time, before letting others have their turn.
5. Write the ideas on a whiteboard or flipchart, but don't discuss them at this point.
6. As ideas are shared, individuals can pass if every idea on their list has already been shared, either by themselves or by someone else.
7. Once every idea is listed, run a discussion based on the ideas, or use the ideas to feed a secondary activity, like an affinity diagram or a fishbone diagram.

The nominal group technique is also a good tool to use when the team is stuck or dealing with a particularly difficult concept. The technique helps jar thoughts loose in two ways. First, it removes some of the fear individuals might have about sharing verbal ideas that are still poorly formed. Team members who are writing ideas down can think about them a bit more and may feel more comfortable listing them afterward. Second, the physical act of writing itself has been shown to break through creative and thinking barriers, and can help team members generate more ideas.

### Check Sheets

Check sheets, as a tool, have been mentioned several times throughout this book, but they're worth discussing again more formally. Check sheets are simple tools that can be extremely powerful for managing teams, people, processes, and data. The reason check sheets are so powerful is that they require an action, and when you require a physical, recordable action, personal accountability for that action tends to be higher.

A check sheet is any standardized form used to record information. The information you record might be a specific data point, but it could also be a note that a routine check, analysis, or other task was performed. The purpose of a check sheet, beyond formalizing and requiring an action, is to simplify the process of reporting that action.

Consider the check sheets often seen in restaurant or store public restrooms. These sheets are usually on the door or on the wall near the door. Every hour, an employee signs and dates the check sheet to indicate the restroom was checked. By requiring the employee to sign and date the sheet, businesses make it more likely the team will check the restroom at the appropriate times. The signature and date indicate the employee made sure the facility was stocked, clean, and in working order.

This premise can be used across a variety of processes, to make sure data collection or certain tasks are carried out at the right time by the right person. Check sheets can also be used to manage tasks within a project setting — a Six Sigma leader might provide check sheets to each subject-matter expert during a project meeting, so each person knows what needs to be done before the next meeting and has a physical record requirement.

As a Six Sigma specialist, it's important to understand when the simplest solution meets your need, and the check sheet is often that solution.

### SWOT Analysis

SWOT analysis is a common business brainstorming technique that helps teams understand, at a high level, strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats — or challenges — for a project, improvement, or process. SWOT analyses can be run at any point during the DMAIC phases, but are especially useful during the Define phase, or whenever the team has hit conflict (storming) and needs something quick and easy to help get back on track.

Some people lay out the SWOT analysis in a visual representation, drawing a large four-square grid, one for each element: Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, and Threats. This can be useful if you have an especially visual project group, but it isn't necessary. The goal of a SWOT analysis is really to answer a few fundamental questions through brainstorming.

1. **Strengths:** What works within the process? What's done better, faster, cheaper, more uniquely?
2. **Weaknesses:** What doesn't work? What are the drawbacks, problems, losses, errors, or points of customer dissatisfaction?
3. **Opportunities:** What can be fixed? What are some easy problems to fix? Where are improvements needed?
4. **Threats:** What obstacles exist to improvement? What risks will the project team face? What resource challenges might exist?

### Starburst Brainstorming

Starburst brainstorming is a method for generating a series of questions about a problem, process, or idea. These questions can later be used to define processes, problems, products, or other ideas. On the surface, the starburst tool is similar to the 5 Whys, but instead of answering each question and then asking another, the team simply tries to come up with as many different questions as possible.

Run a starburst brainstorming session by following these steps:

1. Draw a six-pointed star on a whiteboard or large piece of paper.
2. On each of the points, write one of the following words: Who, What, Where, When, Why, How.
3. In the center of the star, write a word or a few words describing the central idea.
4. For each point of the star, brainstorm questions about the center that start with that point's word. For example, a team might be working to increase customer satisfaction with a food-service product. For this example's purposes, imagine a team working to solve a customer satisfaction problem with an individually wrapped snack cake, typically sold at convenience stores and newsstands.
   a. The center of the star might simply say "ABC Snack Cake."
   b. Questions on the star's "Who?" point could include:
      i. Who's the snack cake's primary customer?
      ii. Who's most likely to eat the snack cake?
      iii. Who's going to buy the snack cake? (not always the same person who eats it)
      iv. Who's going to sell the snack cake?
      v. Who's going to market the snack cake?
      vi. Who's going to manufacture the snack cake?
   c. "What?" questions could include:
      i. What flavor, or flavors, should the snack cake have?
      ii. What packaging is best for the snack cake?
      iii. What ingredients matter for the snack cake?
   d. Work through every point of the star, asking questions that match that point's word. Generate as many questions as possible within a set time period. It's a good idea to set a time limit for question generation at each point of the star — up to five minutes usually works well — to keep the questions from getting too detailed or straying outside the scope of the problem, process, or idea you're dealing with.

The purpose of the starburst session isn't to answer the questions that come up, and that can be a challenge for Six Sigma leaders. Team members will naturally want to jump straight from a question to an answer, which can derail the process and result in an unproductive or out-of-scope discussion. Steer team members back toward asking questions throughout the brainstorming session. These questions can later be compiled and used when running other exercises, like SIPOCs or process maps. The questions help ensure no detail is left out, and that every possible issue is considered.

### Role-Play (or Figuring) Brainstorming

One of the biggest challenges with brainstorming on a Six Sigma team is that, after a few meetings, or as the team digs deeper into the DMAIC process, it can get stuck on certain beliefs and ideas. Once certain ideas are proposed, it can be hard to "step away" from them. Teams may find themselves repeatedly coming back to the same ideas. Sometimes, this means the team is on the right track, and the repetition of the same concepts throughout the DMAIC process and brainstorming confirms these are the right things to think about. Other times, though, it can be a sign the team is stuck.

It can be hard to tell the difference sometimes, and Six Sigma specialists need to rely on analysis and data to help decide whether the team is heading the right direction or not. If a Six Sigma specialist believes the team isn't heading the right direction, they can try role-play brainstorming, to try to get team members thinking more creatively or from a different perspective on the issue.

Role-play brainstorming can be combined with many of this chapter's other tools to generate new thinking. Pick one of the simpler brainstorming exercises, or simply ask a question and have people brainstorm answers. However, ask participants to brainstorm as if they were someone else, not themselves. They could brainstorm as the company's CEO. They could brainstorm as a person working on the production line. They could brainstorm as Johnny Depp, the President of the United States, or Cookie Monster.

This is where Six Sigma leadership matters. Will the group likely respond better to a more relaxed situation, one that breaks down some of the barriers they've built up, or will it respond better to a more serious role-play scenario? That helps you decide between Cookie Monster and the CEO.

One challenge with this kind of team activity is balancing the stress relief and creativity of the more relaxed activity against the real need to be productive. If things are degenerating into pure fun with no productivity, then the Six Sigma team leader should end the activity and move on to something else. Time usually isn't wasted, though — stepping away from the project's seriousness for a few minutes is often enough, on its own, to help teams think more creatively.

### Brainwriting

Brainwriting is, in a way, similar to the nominal group technique. In fact, the nominal group technique is itself a form of brainwriting. Reasons to build this kind of brainstorming into your meetings include boosting input from quieter or more reserved members, reducing how much just one or two more talkative members impact a meeting's outcome, and generating ideas other brainstorming methods aren't generating. Remember, the physical act of writing itself contributes to thought processes and can help the brain make connections between ideas it would be less likely to make during verbal brainstorming.

There are several types of brainwriting exercises you can use in a team setting. The nominal group technique is one of them, and this section provides a few other options.

**The Brainwriting Pool Method**

The pool method can help generate different ideas, because participants build on each other's ideas, without the pressure of a fast-paced verbal brainstorming session. Each participant gets a piece of paper and a pen. You can print the pages with a question or idea at the top, or state the prompt for the session once everyone is ready. Each person writes two to three ideas on their paper, then places the paper back in the center of the table. Each person picks up another paper from the pool (one that already has ideas written by someone else) and adds two or three more ideas. Papers are written on, returned, and picked up again, repeatedly. There are no timed rounds — each participant moves at their own pace and pulls from the central pool as pages become available.

At the end of the exercise, which runs for a predetermined time, the team logs every idea on a single page or whiteboard, and categorizes and organizes them appropriately. The session's length will depend on how many people are involved and the problem's complexity. A good time limit for this exercise is usually between 10 and 30 minutes, and the exercise works best with four to eight participants.

**The Brainwriting Card Method**

Often, the goal of brainwriting is to build on each other's ideas, which is achieved by returning to and picking up pages from the pool, in the method above. The card method uses a similar approach, but logs each idea on a separate card, for more flexibility during the exercise's analysis or categorization part.

The card method works well with groups of four to eight people. Start by giving each participant a stack of index cards and a pen. Present a question or problem — sometimes it helps to write that question or problem on a whiteboard or large piece of paper, so participants can refer back to it throughout the exercise.

Participants start by brainstorming their own ideas, writing each idea on one of the cards. After an idea is written, the card containing that idea is passed to the left. Once a participant has written down as many ideas as they can quickly think of, they start picking up and reading the cards passed to them by the person on their right.

If a participant can add something to any card's idea that they read, they write the new or extended idea on a new card and attach it to the existing card. Those cards are then passed to the left. If the participant can't add anything new, the cards are simply passed to the left.

When a participant receives their own cards back, they hold onto them. The brainwriting session ends when every participant has gotten back all of their original cards, hopefully now with attachments from other ideas. The facilitator then collects the cards, and they can be used for further brainstorming and idea organization. You could use the cards to build an affinity diagram, for example.

The brainwriting card method is also a good way to kick off a group effort to build a process map. Instead of writing solution ideas for a problem, the team writes down individual pieces of a process — including activities, inputs, and outputs. Those pieces can then form the basic structure of a process map, which the team can build on further.

### Brainstorming Alone

This chapter, and most of the information throughout this book, focuses on activities and methods for use in a group setting. That's because tackling and solving problems as a team is a fundamental part of the Six Sigma methodology. Team brainstorming is essential because it brings multiple perspectives and lets individual team members build thoughts on top of ideas generated by others. However, it isn't always possible, or even a good idea, to brainstorm every issue as a group.

Sometimes, the Six Sigma leader needs to consider an issue or idea before presenting it to the group. Other times, the issue you want to brainstorm isn't something appropriate to share with the whole team. Remember, if you're in a Black Belt or project leadership role, you may have access to sensitive or confidential information. Although Six Sigma projects and process improvement work function best in transparent settings, it simply isn't always possible for every member of a Six Sigma team to know every piece of information about a process. As a Six Sigma leader, you should work to build a team you feel is capable of appropriately handling sensitive information, but you should also be prepared to facilitate a team in unique situations, when sharing some information is limited. This can be especially true in sectors like healthcare or finance, where the data itself is sensitive.

There are other reasons to brainstorm alone, as a project leader or Six Sigma specialist. Your team might be stalling because of internal conflict (storming) or runaway scope creep, two challenges covered in earlier units. You may want to arrive at a team meeting prepared with a few ideas or an understanding of the problem — though you should always be careful not to steer others too closely toward your own ideas, since that can reduce the team's effectiveness. As a Six Sigma specialist, you may also face your own problems or information needs outside a team setting.

Whatever the reason, you can use shortened forms of many of this chapter's brainstorming tools to brainstorm alone. Tools like starburst brainstorming, SWOT analysis, and force field analysis can be run individually. For example, if your team seems stuck at a certain DMAIC phase, you could use force field analysis to help identify which problems or people are holding you back. As a Six Sigma leader, you can then use that information to address the issues, so the team can move forward with a project.

Brainstorming is a powerful tool, whether used as a team or individually. It takes practice to be able to best implement brainstorming methods across various group dynamics, but by following this chapter's basic guidelines, you'll almost always get at least some positive result from a brainstorming session.
